\section{Introduction}

A quantum group is not a group. It is a deformation of the algebra of symmetries of a group,
depending on a parameter $q$, which recovers the classical object at $q=1$ but which carries,
away from that point, an extra piece of structure: a braiding. The purpose of this paper is to
make each step of that sentence precise and provable for $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{sl}_2$, and to
follow the consequences to a computation that distinguishes the trefoil knot from the unknot.

The narrative has four movements: \emph{deformation} (the algebra $\Uq$, its Casimir, its
modules, its higher commutators and its deformed binomial calculus); \emph{degeneration} (every
deformed quantity converges to its classical counterpart as $q\to1$, the delicate case being a
quotient of two vanishing quantities); \emph{braiding} (the extra structure, in the form of the
Temperley--Lieb algebra and the Kauffman $R$-matrix); and \emph{topology} (closing braids with
the quantum trace, and the resulting invariant of the $(2,n)$ torus links).

Throughout, $k$ is a field (in analytic statements $\mathbb R$) and $\mathcal A$ an associative
unital $k$-algebra.

\section{Quantum integers}

\begin{definition}\label{def:qint}
For $q\in k^{\times}$ with $q\neq q^{-1}$ and $m\in\mathbb Z$ set
\[
\qint m=\frac{q^{m}-q^{-m}}{q-q^{-1}}.
\]
\end{definition}

Thus $\qint 0=0$, $\qint 1=1$, $\qint{-m}=-\qint m$ and $\qint 2=q+q^{-1}$.

\begin{theorem}[Fundamental quadratic identity]\label{thm:qid}
For all $a,b\in\mathbb Z$ and $q\in k^{\times}$,
\[
\qint a\,\qint b-\qint{a-1}\,\qint{b+1}=\qint{b-a+1}.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Clear denominators; the claim becomes the Laurent-polynomial identity
\[
(q^{a}-q^{-a})(q^{b}-q^{-b})-(q^{a-1}-q^{1-a})(q^{b+1}-q^{-b-1})
=(q^{b-a+1}-q^{a-b-1})(q-q^{-1}).
\]
The first product equals $q^{a+b}-q^{a-b}-q^{b-a}+q^{-a-b}$ and the second equals
$q^{a+b}-q^{a-b-2}-q^{b-a+2}+q^{-a-b}$, so the left side is
$q^{b-a+2}-q^{b-a}+q^{a-b-2}-q^{a-b}$, which is the expansion of the right side. If $q=q^{-1}$
all quantum integers vanish and the identity is trivial.
\end{proof}

Theorem~\ref{thm:qid} is the arithmetic engine of the subject: it is precisely the statement
that the commutator of the deformed raising and lowering operators closes on a Cartan-type
operator.

\begin{theorem}[Denominator-free form]\label{thm:reg}
For $q\neq0$ with $q^{2}\neq1$ and $m\in\mathbb N$,
$\displaystyle \qint m=q^{\,1-m}\sum_{i=0}^{m-1}q^{2i}.$
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Write $q-q^{-1}=q^{-1}(q^{2}-1)$ and $q^{m}-q^{-m}=q^{-m}\bigl((q^{2})^{m}-1\bigr)$, and apply
the geometric-sum identity $\bigl(\sum_{i<m}(q^{2})^{i}\bigr)(q^{2}-1)=(q^{2})^{m}-1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}\label{cor:qintlim}
For every $m\in\mathbb Z$, $\qint m\to m$ as $q\to1$ in $\mathbb R$ (along $q\neq1$).
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
For $m\ge0$ the right-hand side of Theorem~\ref{thm:reg} is continuous at $q=1$ with value $m$,
and the two expressions agree on a punctured neighbourhood of $1$. For $m<0$ use
$\qint{-m}=-\qint m$.
\end{proof}

\section{The deformed algebra $\Uq$}

\begin{definition}\label{def:uq}
Let $q\in k$ with $q\neq0$, $q^{2}\neq1$. Elements $E,F,K,\bar K\in\mathcal A$ \emph{present}
$\Uq$ if
\[
K\bar K=\bar KK=1,\qquad KE=q^{2}EK,\qquad q^{2}KF=FK,\qquad
EF-FE=\frac{K-\bar K}{q-q^{-1}} .
\]
We write $\bar K=K^{-1}$. Note $q^{2}\ne1$ forces $q-q^{-1}\ne0$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}
Elements $e,f,h$ \emph{present} $\Ucl$ if $he-eh=2e$, $hf-fh=-2f$, $ef-fe=h$.
\end{definition}

\subsection{The quantum Casimir}

\begin{definition}
$\displaystyle C_{q}=FE+\frac{qK+q^{-1}K^{-1}}{(q-q^{-1})^{2}}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Centrality]\label{thm:central}
If $E,F,K,K^{-1}$ present $\Uq$, then $C_{q}$ commutes with $E$, with $F$ and with $K$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
From $KE=q^{2}EK$ one gets $EK=q^{-2}KE$ and $EK^{-1}=q^{2}K^{-1}E$; symmetrically $FK=q^{2}KF$
and $FK^{-1}=q^{-2}K^{-1}F$. Expanding $C_{q}E-EC_{q}$, the term $FE\cdot E-E\cdot FE$ equals
$-(EF-FE)E=-(q-q^{-1})^{-1}(K-K^{-1})E$, while commuting $E$ through the Cartan part produces
the scalars $q(1-q^{-2})/(q-q^{-1})^{2}=(q-q^{-1})^{-1}$ and
$q^{-1}(1-q^{2})/(q-q^{-1})^{2}=-(q-q^{-1})^{-1}$, which cancel it exactly. The $F$-case is the
mirror image, and the $K$-case follows since $K$ commutes with the Cartan part and
$KFE=q^{-2}q^{2}FEK=FEK$.
\end{proof}

The classical shadow: for $e,f,h$ presenting $\Ucl$ and $\operatorname{char}k\ne2$, the element
$C=fe+\tfrac14h^{2}+\tfrac12h$ is central.

\subsection{Finite-dimensional modules}

Fix $n\in\mathbb N$ and define operators on the ladder $v_{0},\dots,v_{n}$ by
\[
E\,v_{i}=\qint i\,v_{i-1},\qquad F\,v_{i}=\qint{n-i}\,v_{i+1},\qquad
K\,v_{i}=q^{\,n-2i}v_{i},\qquad K^{-1}v_{i}=q^{-(n-2i)}v_{i}.
\]

\begin{theorem}\label{thm:module}
For every admissible $q$ and every $n$ these operators present $\Uq$, and the span of
$v_{0},\dots,v_{n}$ is invariant under all four.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The Cartan relations are immediate from the exponents. The commutator relation is
Theorem~\ref{thm:qid} with $a=i$, $b=n-i$:
\[
\qint i\,\qint{n-i+1}-\qint{n-i}\,\qint{i+1}=\qint{\,n-2i\,}
=\frac{q^{\,n-2i}-q^{-(n-2i)}}{q-q^{-1}},
\]
which is $(K-K^{-1})/(q-q^{-1})$ on $v_{i}$. Invariance holds because $\qint 0=0$ kills $v_{0}$
under $E$ while the coefficient $\qint{n-i}$ vanishes exactly at $i=n$.
\end{proof}

In particular the relations of Definition~\ref{def:uq} are consistent for every admissible $q$.

\subsection{Higher commutators and singular vectors}

\begin{theorem}\label{thm:EFm}
In any presentation of $\Uq$ and for $m\ge1$,
\[
EF^{m}-F^{m}E=\qint m\;F^{m-1}\,\frac{q^{-(m-1)}K-q^{\,m-1}K^{-1}}{q-q^{-1}} .
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Induct on $m$. Moving $K$ past $F^{m}$ costs $q^{-2m}$ and $K^{-1}$ costs $q^{2m}$. The
inductive step reduces to the two scalar recursions
$\qint{m+1}q^{\,m+2}+1=\qint{m+2}q^{\,m+1}$ and
$\qint{m+1}q^{-(m+2)}+1=\qint{m+2}q^{-(m+1)}$, each verified from
Definition~\ref{def:qint} by clearing denominators.
\end{proof}

At $m=2$: $EF^{2}-F^{2}E=(q+q^{-1})F(q^{-1}K-qK^{-1})/(q-q^{-1})$.

\begin{corollary}[Singular vectors]\label{cor:sing}
Let $v$ satisfy $E\cdot v=0$, $K\cdot v=q^{n}v$, $K^{-1}\cdot v=q^{-n}v$. Then
$E\cdot(F^{n+1}v)=0$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:EFm} with $m=n+1$: the term $F^{n+1}Ev$ vanishes, and on $v$ the operator
$q^{-n}K-q^{n}K^{-1}$ acts by $q^{-n}q^{n}-q^{n}q^{-n}=0$.
\end{proof}

The classical shadow of Theorem~\ref{thm:EFm} is
$ef^{m+1}-f^{m+1}e=(m+1)f^{m}h-m(m+1)f^{m}$ in any presentation of $\Ucl$.

\section{Degeneration: $\Uq\to\Ucl$}

Work over $\mathbb R$ and let $q\to1$ with $q\ne1$. Let $e,f,h$ be the classical operators
$e\,v_{i}=i\,v_{i-1}$, $f\,v_{i}=(n-i)v_{i+1}$, $h\,v_{i}=(n-2i)v_{i}$.

\begin{theorem}[Convergence of generators]\label{thm:conv}
For every $n$ the deformed raising and lowering operators converge entrywise to $e$ and $f$, and
\[
\frac{K-K^{-1}}{q-q^{-1}}\;\longrightarrow\;h .
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The first two are Corollary~\ref{cor:qintlim} applied to the coefficients $\qint i$ and
$\qint{n-i}$. For the third, the quotient acts on $v_{i}$ by $\qint{\,n-2i\,}$, which converges
to $n-2i$; the apparent $0/0$ is removable.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}\label{thm:limitclassical}
The limiting operators satisfy $ef-fe=h$, $he-eh=2e$, $hf-fh=-2f$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$(ef-fe)v_{i}=\bigl[(i+1)(n-i)-(n-i+1)i\bigr]v_{i}=(n-2i)v_{i}$, and similarly for the others.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Casimir spectrum and its limit}

\begin{theorem}[Quantum Schur's lemma]\label{thm:schur}
On the $(n+1)$-dimensional module $C_{q}$ acts by the scalar
\[
\Omega_{q}(n)=\frac{q^{\,n+1}+q^{-(n+1)}}{(q-q^{-1})^{2}},
\]
independently of the weight.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
On $v_{i}$, $FE$ acts by $\qint{n-i+1}\qint i$ and the Cartan part by
$(q\,q^{\,n-2i}+q^{-1}q^{-(n-2i)})/(q-q^{-1})^{2}$. Clearing $(q-q^{-1})^{2}$, the numerator is
$(q^{\,n-i+1}-q^{-(n-i+1)})(q^{i}-q^{-i})+q^{\,n-2i+1}+q^{-(n-2i+1)}$, whose weight-dependent
terms $-q^{\,n-2i+1}$ and $-q^{-(n-2i+1)}$ cancel against the Cartan contribution, leaving
$q^{\,n+1}+q^{-(n+1)}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Regular form of the shifted eigenvalue]\label{thm:casreg}
For $q\ne0,\pm1$,
\[
\Omega_{q}(n)-\frac{q+q^{-1}}{(q-q^{-1})^{2}}
=q^{\,1-n}\,\frac{\bigl(\sum_{i<n}q^{i}\bigr)\bigl(\sum_{i<n+2}q^{i}\bigr)}{(q+1)^{2}} .
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Substitute $q-q^{-1}=(q^{2}-1)/q$ and $\sum_{i<m}q^{i}=(q^{m}-1)/(q-1)$. The left side becomes
$q^{2}\bigl(q^{\,n+1}+q^{-(n+1)}-q-q^{-1}\bigr)/(q^{2}-1)^{2}$, whose numerator factors as
$q^{1-n}(q^{n}-1)(q^{\,n+2}-1)$; the right side becomes the same expression divided by
$(q-1)^{2}(q+1)^{2}=(q^{2}-1)^{2}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}\label{cor:caslim}
$\displaystyle \Omega_{q}(n)-\frac{q+q^{-1}}{(q-q^{-1})^{2}}\longrightarrow\frac{n(n+2)}{4}$
as $q\to1$: the classical Casimir eigenvalue on the spin-$n/2$ representation.
\end{corollary}

\subsection{Deformed combinatorics}

\begin{definition}
The Gaussian binomials are defined by $\binom{n}{0}_{q}=1$, $\binom{0}{j+1}_{q}=0$ and
$\binom{n+1}{j+1}_{q}=q^{\,n-j}\binom{n}{j}_{q}+\binom{n}{j+1}_{q}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}
$\binom{n}{j}_{q}=0$ for $j>n$; $\binom{n}{n}_{q}=1$; and
$\binom{n}{1}_{q}=1+q+\dots+q^{\,n-1}$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{theorem}[Dual recursion and symmetry]\label{thm:pascal}
For all $n,j$,
\[
\binom{n+1}{j+1}_{q}=\binom{n}{j}_{q}+q^{\,j+1}\binom{n}{j+1}_{q},
\qquad
\binom{n}{j}_{q}=\binom{n}{\,n-j\,}_{q}\quad(j\le n).
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Both by induction on $n$. The base case of the dual recursion is the geometric identity
$\sum_{i<n+2}q^{i}=q\sum_{i<n+1}q^{i}+1=\sum_{i<n+1}q^{i}+q^{\,n+1}$; the inductive step
combines the defining recursion with the hypotheses at $j$ and $j+1$. Symmetry then follows by
expanding $\binom{n+1}{j+1}_{q}$ and $\binom{n+1}{n-j}_{q}$ by the two recursions.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[$q$-binomial theorem]\label{thm:qbinom}
If $yx=q\,(xy)$ in a $k$-algebra, then for all $n$,
\[
(x+y)^{n}=\sum_{j=0}^{n}\binom{n}{j}_{q}\,x^{j}y^{\,n-j}.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
First $y^{m}x=q^{m}xy^{m}$ by induction. Then induct on $n$: right-multiplying the expansion by
$x+y$, the $x$-term contributes $q^{\,n-j}\binom nj_{q}x^{j+1}y^{\,n-j}$ and the $y$-term
$\binom nj_{q}x^{j}y^{\,n-j+1}$; re-indexing, the coefficient of $x^{j+1}y^{\,n-j}$ is
$q^{\,n-j}\binom nj_{q}+\binom n{j+1}_{q}=\binom{n+1}{j+1}_{q}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Degeneration]\label{thm:qbinomlim}
$\binom nj_{1}=\binom nj$; each $\binom nj_{q}$ is a polynomial in $q$, hence continuous, and
$\binom nj_{q}\to\binom nj$ as $q\to1$. Consequently Theorem~\ref{thm:qbinom} collapses at
$q=1$ to the classical binomial theorem.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:bridge}
$\qint m=q^{\,1-m}\binom{m}{1}_{q^{2}}$, and since $KE=q^{2}EK$ is a $q^{2}$-commutation,
Theorem~\ref{thm:qbinom} gives, inside $\Uq$,
\[
(E+K)^{n}=\sum_{j=0}^{n}\binom nj_{q^{2}}E^{j}K^{\,n-j}.
\]
\end{proposition}

\section{Braiding}

\subsection{The invariant singlet}

Let $V=k^{2}$ and take the fundamental representation
\[
E=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix},\quad
F=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\quad
K=\begin{pmatrix}q&0\\0&q^{-1}\end{pmatrix}.
\]

\begin{proposition}
For $q\ne0$, $q^{2}\ne1$, these matrices present $\Uq$.
\end{proposition}

Tensor products use the coproduct
\[
\Delta(E)=E\otimes1+K\otimes E,\qquad
\Delta(F)=F\otimes K^{-1}+1\otimes F,\qquad
\Delta(K)=K\otimes K,
\]
whose asymmetry is the hallmark of the deformation.

\begin{definition}
For $A\in k^{\times}$ with $q=A^{-2}$, the \emph{deformed singlet} is
$\omega=A\,|0\rangle\otimes|1\rangle-A^{-1}|1\rangle\otimes|0\rangle$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Invariance of the singlet]\label{thm:singlet}
With $q=A^{-2}$: $\Delta(E)\omega=0$, $\Delta(F)\omega=0$, $\Delta(K)\omega=\omega$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The two contributions to $\Delta(E)\omega$ are
$(E\otimes1)(-A^{-1}|1\rangle\otimes|0\rangle)=-A^{-1}|0\rangle\otimes|0\rangle$ and
$(K\otimes E)(A|0\rangle\otimes|1\rangle)=Aq\,|0\rangle\otimes|0\rangle$; they cancel exactly
when $Aq=A^{-1}$, i.e.\ $q=A^{-2}$. The $F$-case is the mirror computation with $K^{-1}$, and
$\Delta(K)$ scales both terms by $q\cdot q^{-1}=1$.
\end{proof}

Theorem~\ref{thm:singlet} says $V\otimes V$ contains a trivial submodule, so equivariant
\emph{cup} and \emph{cap} maps exist, and their composite is an invariant endomorphism of
$V\otimes V$.

\subsection{Temperley--Lieb algebras and the Kauffman braiding}

\begin{definition}
The \emph{loop value} is $\delta=-A^{2}-A^{-2}$. Elements $e_{1},e_{2}$ form a
\emph{Temperley--Lieb pair} if
$e_{i}^{2}=\delta e_{i}$, $e_{1}e_{2}e_{1}=e_{1}$, $e_{2}e_{1}e_{2}=e_{2}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}
With $q=A^{-2}$ one has $\delta=-\qint2$: the loop value is minus the quantum dimension of the
fundamental representation.
\end{proposition}

\begin{theorem}[Explicit realisation]\label{thm:TL8}
Let $c(0,1)=A$, $c(1,0)=-A^{-1}$ and $c=0$ otherwise. On $V^{\otimes3}$ define $8\times8$
matrices
\[
(e_{1})_{p,r}=-c(p_{1},p_{2})c(r_{1},r_{2})\,\delta_{p_{3}r_{3}},\qquad
(e_{2})_{p,r}=-\delta_{p_{1}r_{1}}\,c(p_{2},p_{3})c(r_{2},r_{3}).
\]
Then $(e_{1},e_{2})$ is a Temperley--Lieb pair for every $A\ne0$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The scalar inputs are $\sum_{i,j}c(i,j)^{2}=A^{2}+A^{-2}=-\delta$, giving
$e_{i}^{2}=\delta e_{i}$, and the contraction $\sum_{j}c(i,j)c(j,l)=-\delta_{il}$, giving the
zig-zag identities.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}
For $e$ with $e^{2}=\delta e$ put $g=A\cdot1+A^{-1}e$ and $\bar g=A^{-1}\cdot1+A\,e$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Reidemeister II]\label{thm:RII}
$g\bar g=\bar gg=1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$g\bar g=1+(A^{2}+A^{-2})e+e^{2}=1+(A^{2}+A^{-2}+\delta)e=1$.
\end{proof}

Thus the loop value is \emph{forced}: $g$ has the mirror-image inverse exactly when
$\delta=-A^{2}-A^{-2}$.

\begin{theorem}[Braid relation / Yang--Baxter equation]\label{thm:YBE}
For a Temperley--Lieb pair and $g_{i}=A+A^{-1}e_{i}$, $\;g_{1}g_{2}g_{1}=g_{2}g_{1}g_{2}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Expand the eight terms of $g_{1}g_{2}g_{1}$. Four are $A^{3}\cdot1$, $A\,e_{2}$,
$A^{-1}e_{1}e_{2}$, $A^{-1}e_{2}e_{1}$; the other four are multiples of $e_{1}$ with total
coefficient $2A+A^{-1}\delta+A^{-3}=A$, using $e_{1}^{2}=\delta e_{1}$ and
$e_{1}e_{2}e_{1}=e_{1}$. The normal form
$A^{3}+A e_{1}+A e_{2}+A^{-1}e_{1}e_{2}+A^{-1}e_{2}e_{1}$ is symmetric in $e_{1}\leftrightarrow
e_{2}$, and the expansion of $g_{2}g_{1}g_{2}$ gives the same expression.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}\label{cor:braidrep}
Let $B_{3}=\langle\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2}\mid
\sigma_{1}\sigma_{2}\sigma_{1}=\sigma_{2}\sigma_{1}\sigma_{2}\rangle$. Every Temperley--Lieb
pair determines a homomorphism $B_{3}\to R^{\times}$, $\sigma_{i}\mapsto g_{i}$; with
Theorem~\ref{thm:TL8} this gives an $8$-dimensional representation of $B_{3}$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{theorem}[Naturality]\label{thm:natural}
Let $e$ be the Temperley--Lieb generator on $V\otimes V$, $e_{p,r}=-c(p_{1},p_{2})c(r_{1},r_{2})$,
and $q=A^{-2}$. Then $e$ commutes with $\Delta(E)$, $\Delta(F)$, $\Delta(K)$; hence
$\check R=A\cdot1+A^{-1}e$ is a morphism of $\Uq$-modules.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$e$ is, up to scale, the composite of the equivariant cap and cup of
Theorem~\ref{thm:singlet}; the four commutators are verified entrywise, the substitution
$q=A^{-2}$ being exactly what each requires. Linearity gives the statement for $\check R$.
\end{proof}

\section{The invariant of the $(2,n)$ torus links}

\begin{theorem}[Temperley--Lieb expansion]\label{thm:expand}
Let $e^{2}=\delta e$ and $g=A+A^{-1}e$. Then $g^{n}=A^{n}\cdot1+b_{n}e$, where $b_{0}=0$ and
$b_{n+1}=Ab_{n}+A^{-1}A^{n}+A^{-1}\delta b_{n}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Closed form]\label{thm:closed}
For $A\ne0$ and all $n$, $\;\delta\,b_{n}=(-1)^{n}A^{-3n}-A^{n}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Induction. Multiplying the recursion by $\delta$ and using
$A+A^{-1}\delta=-A^{-3}$ gives
$\delta b_{n+1}=-A^{-3}\bigl((-1)^{n}A^{-3n}-A^{n}\bigr)+A^{n-1}\delta$, and
$A^{n-1}\delta=-A^{n+1}-A^{\,n-3}$; the two $A^{\,n-3}$ terms cancel.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}
On $\operatorname{End}(V\otimes V)$ with $\mu=\operatorname{diag}(-A^{2},-A^{-2})$ set
$\qtr(X)=\sum_{i,j}\mu_{i}\mu_{j}X_{(ij),(ij)}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}\label{thm:qtrace}
$\qtr(1)=\delta^{2}$ and $\qtr(e)=\delta$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$\qtr(1)=(\mu_{0}+\mu_{1})^{2}=\delta^{2}$. The diagonal entries of $e$ are $-c(i,j)^{2}$, and
$\mu_{0}\mu_{1}=1$, so $\qtr(e)=-(A^{2}+A^{-2})=\delta$.
\end{proof}

Diagrammatically: the closure of the identity braid is a two-component unlink, that of $e$ a
single circle.

\begin{definition}\label{def:bracket}
The \emph{Kauffman bracket} of the closure of $\sigma_{1}^{n}$ (the $(2,n)$ torus link) is
$\langle n\rangle=A^{n}\delta+b_{n}$, and the writhe-corrected invariant is
$V_{n}=(-A^{-3})^{n}\langle n\rangle$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Consistency with the $R$-matrix]\label{thm:consistency}
$\qtr(\check R^{\,n})=\delta\,\langle n\rangle$, hence
$V_{n}=(-A^{-3})^{n}\qtr(\check R^{\,n})/\delta$ for $\delta\ne0$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Apply $\qtr$ to Theorem~\ref{thm:expand} and use Theorem~\ref{thm:qtrace}:
$\qtr(g^{n})=A^{n}\delta^{2}+b_{n}\delta$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Closed form of the bracket]\label{thm:bracketclosed}
$\delta\,\langle n\rangle=\delta^{2}A^{n}+(-1)^{n}A^{-3n}-A^{n}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Normalisation]\label{thm:unknot}
$V_{1}=1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$b_{1}=A^{-1}$, so $\langle1\rangle=A\delta+A^{-1}=-A^{3}$ and $V_{1}=(-A^{-3})(-A^{3})=1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Hopf link and trefoil]\label{thm:trefoil}
$\langle2\rangle=-A^{4}-A^{-4}$ and $\langle3\rangle=-A^{5}-A^{-3}+A^{-7}$; consequently, with
$t=A^{-4}$,
\[
V_{3}=t+t^{3}-t^{4}.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$b_{2}=2+A^{-2}\delta=1-A^{-4}$, so $\langle2\rangle=A^{2}\delta+b_{2}=-A^{4}-A^{-4}$;
similarly $b_{3}=Ab_{2}+A+A^{-1}\delta b_{2}$ gives
$\langle3\rangle=A^{3}\delta+b_{3}=-A^{5}-A^{-3}+A^{-7}$, and multiplying by
$(-A^{-3})^{3}=-A^{-9}$ yields $A^{-4}+A^{-12}-A^{-16}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[The trefoil is knotted]\label{cor:knotted}
$V_{3}\ne V_{1}$ as functions of $A$: at $A=2$ one has $t=1/16$ and
$V_{3}=4111/65536\ne1$.
\end{corollary}

Combined with the algebraic Reidemeister identities (Theorem~\ref{thm:RII} for move~II and
Theorem~\ref{thm:YBE} for move~III), which show the bracket is unchanged under the diagram moves
relating equivalent links, this is the classical proof that the trefoil cannot be unknotted.

\begin{remark}[Scope]
We take the trace formula of Definition~\ref{def:bracket} as the definition of the invariant of
the closed braid $\sigma_{1}^{n}$; the diagrammatic verification of Reidemeister invariance for
general diagrams is a separate topological step. What is established here is the complete
algebra: the exact expansion, the closed form for every $n$, the identification of the abstract
trace with the quantum trace of the $R$-matrix, and the separation of the trefoil from the
unknot.
\end{remark}

\section{Quantum doubles and braided structure}

\begin{definition}
A binary operation $\triangleright$ on a set $X$ is \emph{self-distributive} if
$x\triangleright(y\triangleright z)=(x\triangleright y)\triangleright(x\triangleright z)$.
\end{definition}

Define $c_{1},c_{2}:X^{3}\to X^{3}$ by $c_{1}(x,y,z)=(x\triangleright y,x,z)$ and
$c_{2}(x,y,z)=(x,y\triangleright z,y)$.

\begin{theorem}\label{thm:rack}
$c_{1}c_{2}c_{1}=c_{2}c_{1}c_{2}$ if and only if $\triangleright$ is self-distributive.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The second and third coordinates of both composites agree automatically; the first coordinates
are $x\triangleright(y\triangleright z)$ and
$(x\triangleright y)\triangleright(x\triangleright z)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}\label{cor:double}
In any group $G$, conjugation $x\triangleright y=xyx^{-1}$ is self-distributive; $c_{1},c_{2}$
are bijections of $G^{3}$ and define a homomorphism
$B_{3}\to\operatorname{Sym}(G^{3})$, $\sigma_{i}\mapsto c_{i}$.
\end{corollary}

This is the canonical Yetter--Drinfeld structure of the quantum double $D(k[G])$, made
elementary.

\begin{definition}
For a finite abelian group $A$, a \emph{bicharacter} is $\chi:A\times A\to\mathbb C$ with
$\chi(x+y,z)=\chi(x,z)\chi(y,z)$, $\chi(x,y+z)=\chi(x,y)\chi(x,z)$, $\chi(x,0)=1$. It is
\emph{nondegenerate} if for each $x\ne0$ there is $y$ with $\chi(x,y)\ne1$.
\end{definition}

The anyon braiding acts on coefficient functions on $A^{3}$ by
$(c_{1}f)(x,y,z)=\chi(y,x)f(y,x,z)$ and $(c_{2}f)(x,y,z)=\chi(z,y)f(x,z,y)$.

\begin{theorem}\label{thm:anyon}
$c_{1}c_{2}c_{1}=c_{2}c_{1}c_{2}$ for every $\chi$, and the two bilinearity axioms are exactly
the left and right hexagon identities relating braiding to fusion.
\end{theorem}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:chizero}
$\chi(0,y)=1$ for all $y$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{theorem}[Modularity]\label{thm:modular}
Let $\chi$ be nondegenerate, $S_{xy}=\chi(x,y)$ and $S'_{y,x'}=\chi(-x',y)$. Then
\[
\sum_{y\in A}\chi(x,y)\chi(-x',y)=
\begin{cases}|A|,&x=x',\\0,&x\ne x',\end{cases}
\qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad SS'=|A|\cdot\id .
\]
In particular $S$ is invertible.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
By bilinearity the summand is $\psi(y)$ with $\psi=\chi(x-x',\cdot)$ an additive character.
Character orthogonality gives $|A|$ if $\psi$ is trivial and $0$ otherwise; triviality for
$x=x'$ is Lemma~\ref{lem:chizero}, and nontriviality for $x\ne x'$ is nondegeneracy applied to
$x-x'\ne0$.
\end{proof}

Invertibility of $S$ is the defining property of a \emph{modular} tensor category: no nontrivial
object is transparent to the braiding.

\section{Algorithms}

\textbf{Algorithm A (bracket by recursion).} Given $A,n$: set $\delta=-A^{2}-A^{-2}$, $b:=0$;
for $i=0,\dots,n-1$ set $b:=Ab+A^{-1}A^{i}+A^{-1}\delta b$; return
$\langle n\rangle=A^{n}\delta+b$ and $V_{n}=(-A^{-3})^{n}\langle n\rangle$. Cost $O(n)$;
correctness is Theorems~\ref{thm:expand} and~\ref{thm:closed}, and the closed form gives an
$O(\log n)$ alternative and an independent check.

\textbf{Algorithm B (quantum trace of the $R$-matrix).} Build the $4\times4$ matrix $e$ from the
cup coefficients, form $\check R=A\cdot1+A^{-1}e$, compute $\check R^{\,n}$ by repeated
squaring, and return $\sum_{i,j}\mu_{i}\mu_{j}(\check R^{\,n})_{(ij),(ij)}$. Cost $O(\log n)$
multiplications of fixed size; by Theorem~\ref{thm:consistency} the output is
$\delta\langle n\rangle$.

\textbf{Algorithm C (degeneration scan).} For $q\to1$, tabulate $\qint m$ against $m$,
$\binom nj_{q}$ against $\binom nj$, and the shifted Casimir eigenvalue against $n(n+2)/4$. The
last is a difference of two quantities of size $\Theta((q-1)^{-2})$ and should be evaluated
through the regular form of Theorem~\ref{thm:casreg} when $|q-1|$ is small.

\section{Discussion}

The classical algebra is cocommutative: the flip identifies the two orders of a tensor product
and squares to the identity. The deformation breaks cocommutativity --- visibly, in
$\Delta(E)=E\otimes1+K\otimes E$ --- and the price of restoring an isomorphism
$V\otimes W\cong W\otimes V$ is that it is no longer an involution. That failure is the
braiding, and Theorem~\ref{thm:YBE} is its coherence condition. At $q=1$ the braiding degenerates
to the flip; Theorems~\ref{thm:conv}, \ref{thm:limitclassical}, \ref{thm:qbinomlim} and
Corollary~\ref{cor:caslim} confirm nothing else is lost.

The loop value is not a choice. Theorem~\ref{thm:RII} forces $\delta=-A^{2}-A^{-2}$ for the
braiding to be invertible with its mirror image, and the writhe factor $-A^{-3}$ of
Definition~\ref{def:bracket} is exactly what cancels the kink factor $A\delta+A^{-1}=-A^{3}$ of
Theorem~\ref{thm:unknot}. Two scalar equations in one unknown: topological invariance is
downstream of their simultaneous solvability.

Limitations: the invariant is computed for the two-strand family, with the trace formula taken
as the definition of the closed-braid invariant; the classical-limit statements are proved at
the level of explicit finite-dimensional modules and structure constants rather than for a flat
family of algebras over a formal parameter; and modularity is proved in the pointed (abelian)
case, a model for --- not a proof of --- the root-of-unity statement for $\Uq$.

\section{Future directions}

\begin{conjecture}[Rigidity of the loop value]
Let $R$ contain $e$ with $e^{2}=\delta e$, put $g=A+A^{-1}e$ and define a Markov-style functional
by $\operatorname{tr}(1)=\delta$, $\operatorname{tr}(e)=1$. Then $(-A^{-3})^{w}\operatorname{tr}(g^{n})$
is invariant under all three Reidemeister moves if and only if $\delta=-A^{2}-A^{-2}$. The loop
value enters only through $A\delta+A^{-1}=-A^{3}$ and
$A\cdot A^{-1}+A^{-1}A+A^{-1}\delta A^{-1}=0$, simultaneously solvable only at that value.
\end{conjecture}

\begin{conjecture}[Completeness of the $(2,n)$ family]
$n\mapsto V_{n}(A)$ is injective on $\mathbb N$ for every transcendental $A$, and already at
$A=2$, where $V_{1}=1$, $V_{3}=4111/65536$, $V_{5}=1052431/268435456$. The closed form makes
$V_{n}(2)$ a sequence of rationals with denominators $2^{4n}$, so injectivity should reduce to a
valuation argument.
\end{conjecture}

\begin{conjecture}[Unitarity at roots of unity]
For $A=e^{i\theta}$ the $8$-dimensional Temperley--Lieb representation of $B_{3}$ is
unitarisable exactly on the Jones interval, i.e.\ exactly when $|\delta|\le2$, with the
invariant Hermitian form degenerating at the endpoints.
\end{conjecture}

\begin{conjecture}[Quantitative classical limit]
The convergence statements admit uniform bounds $|\qint m-m|\le C_{m}|q-1|$ and
$\bigl|\Omega_{q}(n)-(q+q^{-1})/(q-q^{-1})^{2}-n(n+2)/4\bigr|\le C_{n}|q-1|$ with explicit
constants, giving a first-order deformation theory rather than a bare limit.
\end{conjecture}

\begin{conjecture}[Modularity beyond the pointed case]
The orthogonality argument of Theorem~\ref{thm:modular}, applied to the characters of the
Grothendieck ring, yields invertibility of the $S$-matrix for the double of any finite group,
with $|A|$ replaced by $|G|^{2}$ divided by the appropriate centraliser orders.
\end{conjecture}

\section{Conclusion}

Bending a symmetry algebra by one parameter has three consequences. Nothing is lost: quantum
integers, Gaussian binomials, finite-dimensional modules and Casimir eigenvalues all converge to
their classical counterparts as $q\to1$, including a $0/0$ Cartan quotient with a perfectly
regular limit. Something is gained: an invariant, non-involutive exchange operator satisfying the
Yang--Baxter equation, hence braid group representations. And the gain is computable: closing
two-strand braids with the quantum trace yields the exact bracket of every $(2,n)$ torus link,
correctly normalised on the unknot and giving $t+t^{3}-t^{4}$ for the trefoil --- a number,
$4111/65536$ at $t=1/16$, that certifies a piece of string cannot be untied.

Complex = complex
Matrix = List[List[complex]]


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Quantum integers
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def q_int(q: float, m: int) -> float:
    """Symmetric quantum integer [m]_q = (q^m - q^-m)/(q - q^-1)."""
    return (q ** m - q ** (-m)) / (q - 1.0 / q)


def q_int_regular(q: float, m: int) -> float:
    """Denominator-free form  [m]_q = q^{1-m} * sum_{i<m} q^{2i}  (m >= 0)."""
    return q ** (1 - m) * sum(q ** (2 * i) for i in range(m))


def demo_quantum_integers() -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("1. QUANTUM INTEGERS DEGENERATE TO ORDINARY INTEGERS")
    print("=" * 74)
    print(f"{'q':>10} | " + " ".join(f"[{m}]_q".rjust(11) for m in range(1, 6)))
    print("-" * 74)
    for q in (1.5, 1.1, 1.01, 1.001, 1.00001):
        row = " ".join(f"{q_int(q, m):11.6f}" for m in range(1, 6))
        print(f"{q:10.5f} | {row}")
    print(f"{'limit':>10} | " + " ".join(f"{m:11.6f}" for m in range(1, 6)))

    # the two formulas agree away from q = 1, and the regular one extends to q = 1
    worst = max(abs(q_int(1.3, m) - q_int_regular(1.3, m)) for m in range(6))
    print(f"\n  max |[m]_q - q^(1-m) sum q^(2i)| at q = 1.3 :  {worst:.3e}")
    print(f"  regular form at q = 1 exactly:  {[q_int_regular(1.0, m) for m in range(6)]}")

    q = 1.234
    err = max(
        abs(q_int(q, a) * q_int(q, b) - q_int(q, a - 1) * q_int(q, b + 1) - q_int(q, b - a + 1))
        for a in range(-3, 4)
        for b in range(-3, 4)
    )
    print(f"  max error in  [a][b] - [a-1][b+1] = [b-a+1]  (|a|,|b| <= 3) :  {err:.3e}")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Gaussian binomials
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def q_binom(q: float, n: int, j: int) -> float:
    """Gaussian binomial via the q-Pascal recursion C_q(n+1,j+1)=q^{n-j}C_q(n,j)+C_q(n,j+1)."""
    if j == 0:
        return 1.0
    if n == 0:
        return 0.0
    return q ** (n - j) * q_binom(q, n - 1, j - 1) + q_binom(q, n - 1, j)


def demo_gaussian_binomials() -> None:
    print()
    print("=" * 74)

        print(f"  q = {q:6.3f} : {vals}")
    print(f"  classical : " + " ".join(f"{comb(n, j):10d}" for j in range(n + 1)))

    # second q-Pascal recursion and reflection symmetry
    q = 1.7

        for j in range(n + 1)
    )
    e2 = max(abs(q_binom(q, n, j) - q_binom(q, n, n - j)) for j in range(n + 1))
    print(f"\n  dual q-Pascal  C(n+1,j+1) = C(n,j) + q^(j+1) C(n,j+1)  error : {e1:.3e}")
    print(f"  reflection symmetry  C(n,j) = C(n,n-j)                 error : {e2:.3e}")

    # q-binomial theorem for q-commuting 2x2 matrices:  y x = q x y
    q = 1.3

    y: Matrix = [[q ** 0.5, 0.0], [0.0, q ** -0.5]]  # a K with K E = q E K

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# small dense matrix helpers
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def mat_add(a: Matrix, b: Matrix) -> Matrix:
    return [[a[i][j] + b[i][j] for j in range(len(a))] for i in range(len(a))]


def mat_sub(a: Matrix, b: Matrix) -> Matrix:
    return [[a[i][j] - b[i][j] for j in range(len(a))] for i in range(len(a))]


def mat_scale(c: complex, a: Matrix) -> Matrix:
    return [[c * a[i][j] for j in range(len(a))] for i in range(len(a))]


def mat_mul(a: Matrix, b: Matrix) -> Matrix:
    n = len(a)
    return [[sum(a[i][k] * b[k][j] for k in range(n)) for j in range(n)] for i in range(n)]


def mat_id(n: int) -> Matrix:
    return [[1.0 if i == j else 0.0 for j in range(n)] for i in range(n)]


def mat_pow(a: Matrix, k: int) -> Matrix:
    out = mat_id(len(a))
    for _ in range(k):
        out = mat_mul(out, a)
    return out


def mat_dist(a: Matrix, b: Matrix) -> float:
    return max(abs(a[i][j] - b[i][j]) for i in range(len(a)) for j in range(len(a)))


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. The (n+1)-dimensional module of U_q(sl_2)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def uq_module(q: float, n: int) -> Tuple[Matrix, Matrix, Matrix, Matrix]:
    """E, F, K, K^-1 on the (n+1)-dimensional highest-weight module, in the basis v_0..v_n.

    E v_i = [i]_q v_{i-1},  F v_i = [n-i]_q v_{i+1},  K v_i = q^{n-2i} v_i.
    """
    d = n + 1
    E = [[0.0] * d for _ in range(d)]
    F = [[0.0] * d for _ in range(d)]
    K = [[0.0] * d for _ in range(d)]
    Ki = [[0.0] * d for _ in range(d)]
    for i in range(d):
        K[i][i] = q ** (n - 2 * i)
        Ki[i][i] = q ** (-(n - 2 * i))
        if i >= 1:
            E[i - 1][i] = q_int(q, i)
        if i + 1 < d:
            F[i + 1][i] = q_int(q, n - i)
    return E, F, K, Ki


def classical_module(n: int) -> Tuple[Matrix, Matrix, Matrix]:
    """e, f, h on the (n+1)-dimensional sl_2 module."""
    d = n + 1
    e = [[0.0] * d for _ in range(d)]
    f = [[0.0] * d for _ in range(d)]
    h = [[0.0] * d for _ in range(d)]
    for i in range(d):
        h[i][i] = float(n - 2 * i)
        if i >= 1:
            e[i - 1][i] = float(i)
        if i + 1 < d:
            f[i + 1][i] = float(n - i)
    return e, f, h


def demo_module_and_limit() -> None:
    print()
    print("=" * 74)
    print("3. THE (n+1)-DIMENSIONAL MODULE, AND ITS CLASSICAL LIMIT")
    print("=" * 74)
    n = 3
    q = 1.4
    E, F, K, Ki = uq_module(q, n)

    rel_KE = mat_dist(mat_mul(K, E), mat_scale(q * q, mat_mul(E, K)))
    rel_KF = mat_dist(mat_scale(q * q, mat_mul(K, F)), mat_mul(F, K))
    cartan = mat_scale(1.0 / (q - 1 / q), mat_sub(K, Ki))
    rel_EF = mat_dist(mat_sub(mat_mul(E, F), mat_mul(F, E)), cartan)
    rel_KK = mat_dist(mat_mul(K, Ki), mat_id(n + 1))
    print(f"  n = {n}, q = {q}")
    print(f"    K K^-1 = 1                          error : {rel_KK:.3e}")
    print(f"    K E = q^2 E K                       error : {rel_KE:.3e}")
    print(f"    q^2 K F = F K                       error : {rel_KF:.3e}")
    print(f"    [E,F] = (K - K^-1)/(q - q^-1)       error : {rel_EF:.3e}")

    e, f, h = classical_module(n)
    print("\n  convergence of the generators to the classical operators:")
    print(f"  {'q':>10} | {'|E-e|':>10} {'|F-f|':>10} {'|cartan-h|':>12}")
    for q in (1.5, 1.1, 1.01, 1.001):
        E, F, K, Ki = uq_module(q, n)
        cartan = mat_scale(1.0 / (q - 1 / q), mat_sub(K, Ki))
        print(f"  {q:10.5f} | {mat_dist(E, e):10.3e} {mat_dist(F, f):10.3e} "
              f"{mat_dist(cartan, h):12.3e}")
    print("  (the Cartan column is the 0/0 quotient (K - K^-1)/(q - q^-1) -> h)")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. The quantum Casimir
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def casimir_scalar(q: float, n: int) -> float:
    """Eigenvalue (q^{n+1} + q^{-(n+1)})/(q - q^-1)^2 of the quantum Casimir."""
    return (q ** (n + 1) + q ** (-(n + 1))) / (q - 1 / q) ** 2


def casimir_regular(q: float, n: int) -> float:
    """Regular form of the shifted eigenvalue: q^{1-n} S_n S_{n+2} / (q+1)^2."""
    sn = sum(q ** i for i in range(n))
    sn2 = sum(q ** i for i in range(n + 2))
    return q ** (1 - n) * sn * sn2 / (q + 1) ** 2


def demo_casimir() -> None:
    print()
    print("=" * 74)
    print("4. THE QUANTUM CASIMIR: SCHUR SCALAR AND CLASSICAL LIMIT")
    print("=" * 74)
    n, q = 3, 1.35
    E, F, K, Ki = uq_module(q, n)
    d = n + 1
    coef = 1.0 / (q - 1 / q) ** 2
    C = mat_add(mat_mul(F, E), mat_scale(coef, mat_add(mat_scale(q, K), mat_scale(1 / q, Ki))))
    lam = casimir_scalar(q, n)
    print(f"  n = {n}, q = {q}:  C - lambda*I  deviation : "
          f"{mat_dist(C, mat_scale(lam, mat_id(d))):.3e}    (lambda = {lam:.6f})")
    print("  => the Casimir acts by ONE scalar on the whole module (quantum Schur)")

    print(f"\n  shifted eigenvalue  Omega_q(n) - (q+q^-1)/(q-q^-1)^2  ->  n(n+2)/4")
    print(f"  {'q':>10} | " + " ".join(f"n={n}".rjust(12) for n in range(1, 5)))
    for q in (1.5, 1.1, 1.01, 1.001):
        shift = (q + 1 / q) / (q - 1 / q) ** 2
        row = " ".join(f"{casimir_scalar(q, n) - shift:12.6f}" for n in range(1, 5))
        print(f"  {q:10.5f} | {row}")
    print(f"  {'limit':>10} | " + " ".join(f"{n * (n + 2) / 4:12.6f}" for n in range(1, 5)))
    q = 1.0001
    err = max(abs(casimir_scalar(q, n) - (q + 1 / q) / (q - 1 / q) ** 2 - casimir_regular(q, n))
              for n in range(1, 5))
    print(f"\n  agreement with the regular form at q = {q} : {err:.3e}"
          "   (regular form is stable, the raw difference is not)")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. Temperley-Lieb, Reidemeister II, Yang-Baxter
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def loop_value(A: complex) -> complex:
    """delta = -A^2 - A^-2."""
    return -A ** 2 - A ** (-2)


def cup(A: complex, i: int, j: int) -> complex:
    """Coefficients of the q-deformed singlet  omega = A|01> - A^-1|10>."""
    if (i, j) == (0, 1):
        return A
    if (i, j) == (1, 0):
        return -1 / A
    return 0.0


def tl_generators_8(A: complex) -> Tuple[Matrix, Matrix]:
    """The 8x8 Temperley-Lieb generators e_1, e_2 on V (x) V (x) V, V = k^2."""
    idx: List[Tuple[int, int, int]] = list(product((0, 1), repeat=3))
    pos: Dict[Tuple[int, int, int], int] = {p: n for n, p in enumerate(idx)}
    e1: Matrix = [[0.0] * 8 for _ in range(8)]
    e2: Matrix = [[0.0] * 8 for _ in range(8)]
    for p in idx:
        for r in idx:
            e1[pos[p]][pos[r]] = -cup(A, p[0], p[1]) * cup(A, r[0], r[1]) * (p[2] == r[2])
            e2[pos[p]][pos[r]] = -cup(A, p[1], p[2]) * cup(A, r[1], r[2]) * (p[0] == r[0])
    return e1, e2


def kauffman(A: complex, e: Matrix) -> Matrix:
    """The braiding g = A*1 + A^-1 e."""
    return mat_add(mat_scale(A, mat_id(len(e))), mat_scale(1 / A, e))


def demo_temperley_lieb() -> None:
    print()
    print("=" * 74)
    print("5. TEMPERLEY-LIEB, REIDEMEISTER II AND THE YANG-BAXTER EQUATION")
    print("=" * 74)
    for A in (2.0, 0.6 + 0.4j, complex(cos(0.7), sin(0.7))):
        e1, e2 = tl_generators_8(A)
        d = loop_value(A)
        s1 = mat_dist(mat_mul(e1, e1), mat_scale(d, e1))
        s2 = mat_dist(mat_mul(e2, e2), mat_scale(d, e2))
        zig = mat_dist(mat_mul(mat_mul(e1, e2), e1), e1)
        zag = mat_dist(mat_mul(mat_mul(e2, e1), e2), e2)
        g1, g2 = kauffman(A, e1), kauffman(A, e2)
        gi1 = mat_add(mat_scale(1 / A, mat_id(8)), mat_scale(A, e1))
        r2 = mat_dist(mat_mul(g1, gi1), mat_id(8))
        ybe = mat_dist(mat_mul(mat_mul(g1, g2), g1), mat_mul(mat_mul(g2, g1), g2))
        print(f"  A = {A!s:>22}   delta = {d:.4f}")
        print(f"    e_i^2 = delta e_i          : {s1:.2e}, {s2:.2e}")
        print(f"    e1e2e1 = e1 , e2e1e2 = e2  : {zig:.2e}, {zag:.2e}")
        print(f"    Reidemeister II  g g' = 1  : {r2:.2e}")
        print(f"    braid relation g1g2g1=g2g1g2: {ybe:.2e}")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 6. The bracket and Jones values of the (2,n) torus links
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def b_coeff(A: Fraction, n: int) -> Fraction:
    """b_n, defined by b_0 = 0 and b_{n+1} = A b_n + A^-1 A^n + A^-1 delta b_n."""
    d = -A ** 2 - 1 / A ** 2
    b = Fraction(0)
    for i in range(n):
        b = A * b + A ** i / A + d * b / A
    return b


def bracket(A: Fraction, n: int) -> Fraction:
    """Kauffman bracket of the closure of sigma_1^n (the (2,n) torus link)."""
    d = -A ** 2 - 1 / A ** 2
    return A ** n * d + b_coeff(A, n)


def jones(A: Fraction, n: int) -> Fraction:
    """Writhe-corrected invariant V_n = (-A^-3)^n <n>."""
    return (-1 / A ** 3) ** n * bracket(A, n)


def qtrace_of_braid_power(A: complex, n: int) -> complex:
    """Quantum trace of R^n on V (x) V, with ribbon weight mu = diag(-A^2, -A^-2)."""
    idx: List[Tuple[int, int]] = list(product((0, 1), repeat=2))
    pos = {p: k for k, p in enumerate(idx)}
    e: Matrix = [[0.0] * 4 for _ in range(4)]
    for p in idx:
        for r in idx:
            e[pos[p]][pos[r]] = -cup(A, p[0], p[1]) * cup(A, r[0], r[1])
    R = mat_pow(kauffman(A, e), n)
    mu = [-A ** 2, -A ** (-2)]
    return sum(mu[p[0]] * mu[p[1]] * R[pos[p]][pos[p]] for p in idx)


def demo_jones() -> None:
    print()
    print("=" * 74)
    print("6. THE (2,n) TORUS LINKS: BRACKET, QUANTUM TRACE, JONES VALUES")
    print("=" * 74)
    A = Fraction(2)
    d = -A ** 2 - 1 / A ** 2
    names = {1: "unknot", 2: "Hopf link", 3: "trefoil", 4: "(2,4) torus link",
             5: "cinquefoil (2,5)"}
    print(f"  exact arithmetic at A = {A}   (delta = {d})")
    print(f"  {'n':>2} {'link':>18} {'<n>':>22} {'V_n':>26}")
    print("  " + "-" * 70)
    for n in range(1, 7):
        print(f"  {n:2d} {names.get(n, f'(2,{n}) torus link'):>18} "
              f"{str(bracket(A, n)):>22} {str(jones(A, n)):>26}")

    # closed form  delta * b_n = (-1)^n A^-3n - A^n
    err = max(abs(d * b_coeff(A, n) - ((-1) ** n / A ** (3 * n) - A ** n)) for n in range(8))
    print(f"\n  closed form  delta*b_n = (-1)^n A^-3n - A^n     max error : {err}")

    # quantum trace of the R-matrix reproduces delta * bracket
    Ac = 0.83 + 0.21j
    dc = loop_value(Ac)
    worst = 0.0
    for n in range(6):

        bn = 0.0 + 0.0j

            bn = Ac * bn + Ac ** i / Ac + dc * bn / Ac
        rhs = dc * (Ac ** n * dc + bn)
        worst = max(worst, abs(lhs - rhs))
    print(f"  qtr(R^n) = delta * <n>  (A = {Ac})   max error : {worst:.3e}")

    # unknot normalisation and the trefoil polynomial, symbolically in t = A^-4
    print(f"\n  V(unknot) = V_1 = {jones(A, 1)}   (must be exactly 1)")
    t = 1 / A ** 4
    print(f"  V(trefoil) = V_3 = {jones(A, 3)}")
    print(f"  t + t^3 - t^4 at t = A^-4 = {t}  =  {t + t ** 3 - t ** 4}")
    print(f"  V_3 == t + t^3 - t^4 ?  {jones(A, 3) == t + t ** 3 - t ** 4}")
    print(f"  V_3 != V_1 ?            {jones(A, 3) != jones(A, 1)}"
          "   ==> the trefoil cannot be untied")

    # check the identity V_3 = t + t^3 - t^4 at several values of A
    bad = [str(a) for a in (Fraction(3), Fraction(5, 2), Fraction(7, 3))

    print(f"  same identity at A = 3, 5/2, 7/3 : {'all hold' if not bad else bad}")

# 7. Quantum double: racks, conjugation, abelian anyons
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def is_self_distributive(elements: Sequence[int], act: Callable[[int, int], int]) -> bool:
    return all(act(x, act(y, z)) == act(act(x, y), act(x, z))
               for x in elements for y in elements for z in elements)


def rack_braid_relation(elements: Sequence[int], act: Callable[[int, int], int]) -> bool:
    def c1(t: Tuple[int, int, int]) -> Tuple[int, int, int]:
        return (act(t[0], t[1]), t[0], t[2])

    def c2(t: Tuple[int, int, int]) -> Tuple[int, int, int]:
        return (t[0], act(t[1], t[2]), t[1])

    return all(c1(c2(c1(t))) == c2(c1(c2(t)))
               for t in product(elements, repeat=3))


def demo_quantum_double() -> None:
    print()
    print("=" * 74)
    print("7. QUANTUM DOUBLE: SELF-DISTRIBUTIVITY, CONJUGATION, MODULARITY")
    print("=" * 74)

    # symmetric group S_3 as permutations of {0,1,2}, conjugation action
    perms: List[Tuple[int, ...]] = sorted(product(range(3), repeat=3))
    perms = [p for p in perms if len(set(p)) == 3]
    index = {p: i for i, p in enumerate(perms)}

    def compose(a: Tuple[int, ...], b: Tuple[int, ...]) -> Tuple[int, ...]:
        return tuple(a[b[i]] for i in range(3))

    def inverse(a: Tuple[int, ...]) -> Tuple[int, ...]:
        out = [0, 0, 0]
        for i, ai in enumerate(a):
            out[ai] = i
        return tuple(out)

    def conj(i: int, j: int) -> int:
        x, y = perms[i], perms[j]
        return index[compose(compose(x, y), inverse(x))]

    elems = list(range(len(perms)))
    print(f"  group S_3 ({len(perms)} elements), action x |> y = x y x^-1")
    print(f"    self-distributive ?      {is_self_distributive(elems, conj)}")
    print(f"    braid relation holds ?   {rack_braid_relation(elems, conj)}")

    # a NON self-distributive operation must fail the braid relation (the 'only if')
    def bad(i: int, j: int) -> int:
        return (i + j) % len(perms)

    print(f"    control: x |> y = x + y  self-distributive ? {is_self_distributive(elems, bad)}"
          f",  braid relation ? {rack_braid_relation(elems, bad)}")

    # abelian anyons: A = Z/N with chi(x,y) = exp(2 pi i x y / N)
    print("\n  abelian anyons  A = Z/N,  chi(x,y) = exp(2 pi i x y / N)")
    for N in (2, 3, 5, 6):
        def chi(x: int, y: int, N: int = N) -> complex:
            return complex(cos(2 * pi * x * y / N), sin(2 * pi * x * y / N))

        # Yang-Baxter for the diagonal braiding
        ybe = max(
            abs(chi(y, x) * chi(z, x) * chi(z, y) - chi(z, y) * chi(z, x) * chi(y, x))
            for x, y, z in product(range(N), repeat=3)
        )
        # hexagons = bilinearity
        hexl = max(abs(chi((x + y) % N, z) - chi(x, z) * chi(y, z))
                   for x, y, z in product(range(N), repeat=3))
        # modularity:  sum_y chi(x,y) chi(-x',y) = N delta_{x,x'}
        worst = 0.0
        for x, xp in product(range(N), repeat=2):
            s = sum(chi(x, y) * chi((-xp) % N, y) for y in range(N))
            target = complex(N if x == xp else 0)
            worst = max(worst, abs(s - target))
        nondeg = all(any(abs(chi(x, y) - 1) > 1e-12 for y in range(N)) for x in range(1, N))
        print(f"    N = {N}:  YBE {ybe:.1e}   hexagon {hexl:.1e}   "
              f"nondegenerate {nondeg}   S S' - N*Id  {worst:.1e}")
    print("  invertible S-matrix  ==>  the braided category is modular")

# 1. Quantum integers
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def q_int(q: float, m: int) -> float:
    """Symmetric quantum integer [m]_q = (q^m - q^-m)/(q - q^-1)."""
    return (q ** m - q ** (-m)) / (q - 1.0 / q)


def q_int_regular(q: float, m: int) -> float:
    """Denominator-free form  [m]_q = q^{1-m} * sum_{i<m} q^{2i}  (m >= 0)."""
    return q ** (1 - m) * sum(q ** (2 * i) for i in range(m))


def demo_quantum_integers() -> None:

    print("1. QUANTUM INTEGERS DEGENERATE TO ORDINARY INTEGERS")
    print("=" * 74)
    print(f"{'q':>10} | " + " ".join(f"[{m}]_q".rjust(11) for m in range(1, 6)))
    print("-" * 74)
    for q in (1.5, 1.1, 1.01, 1.001, 1.00001):
        row = " ".join(f"{q_int(q, m):11.6f}" for m in range(1, 6))
        print(f"{q:10.5f} | {row}")
    print(f"{'limit':>10} | " + " ".join(f"{m:11.6f}" for m in range(1, 6)))

    # the two formulas agree away from q = 1, and the regular one extends to q = 1
    worst = max(abs(q_int(1.3, m) - q_int_regular(1.3, m)) for m in range(6))
    print(f"\n  max |[m]_q - q^(1-m) sum q^(2i)| at q = 1.3 :  {worst:.3e}")
    print(f"  regular form at q = 1 exactly:  {[q_int_regular(1.0, m) for m in range(6)]}")

        for a in range(-3, 4)
        for b in range(-3, 4)
    )
    print(f"  max error in  [a][b] - [a-1][b+1] = [b-a+1]  (|a|,|b| <= 3) :  {err:.3e}")

def q_binom(q: float, n: int, j: int) -> float:
    """Gaussian binomial via the q-Pascal recursion C_q(n+1,j+1)=q^{n-j}C_q(n,j)+C_q(n,j+1)."""
    if j == 0:
        return 1.0
    if n == 0:
        return 0.0
    return q ** (n - j) * q_binom(q, n - 1, j - 1) + q_binom(q, n - 1, j)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# small dense matrix helpers
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def mat_add(a: Matrix, b: Matrix) -> Matrix:
    return [[a[i][j] + b[i][j] for j in range(len(a))] for i in range(len(a))]


def mat_sub(a: Matrix, b: Matrix) -> Matrix:
    return [[a[i][j] - b[i][j] for j in range(len(a))] for i in range(len(a))]


def mat_scale(c: complex, a: Matrix) -> Matrix:
    return [[c * a[i][j] for j in range(len(a))] for i in range(len(a))]


def mat_mul(a: Matrix, b: Matrix) -> Matrix:
    n = len(a)
    return [[sum(a[i][k] * b[k][j] for k in range(n)) for j in range(n)] for i in range(n)]


def mat_id(n: int) -> Matrix:
    return [[1.0 if i == j else 0.0 for j in range(n)] for i in range(n)]


def mat_pow(a: Matrix, k: int) -> Matrix:
    out = mat_id(len(a))
    for _ in range(k):
        out = mat_mul(out, a)
    return out


def mat_dist(a: Matrix, b: Matrix) -> float:
    return max(abs(a[i][j] - b[i][j]) for i in range(len(a)) for j in range(len(a)))


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. The (n+1)-dimensional module of U_q(sl_2)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def uq_module(q: float, n: int) -> Tuple[Matrix, Matrix, Matrix, Matrix]:
    """E, F, K, K^-1 on the (n+1)-dimensional highest-weight module, in the basis v_0..v_n.

    E v_i = [i]_q v_{i-1},  F v_i = [n-i]_q v_{i+1},  K v_i = q^{n-2i} v_i.
    """
    d = n + 1
    E = [[0.0] * d for _ in range(d)]
    F = [[0.0] * d for _ in range(d)]
    K = [[0.0] * d for _ in range(d)]
    Ki = [[0.0] * d for _ in range(d)]
    for i in range(d):
        K[i][i] = q ** (n - 2 * i)
        Ki[i][i] = q ** (-(n - 2 * i))
        if i >= 1:
            E[i - 1][i] = q_int(q, i)
        if i + 1 < d:
            F[i + 1][i] = q_int(q, n - i)
    return E, F, K, Ki


def classical_module(n: int) -> Tuple[Matrix, Matrix, Matrix]:
    """e, f, h on the (n+1)-dimensional sl_2 module."""
    d = n + 1
    e = [[0.0] * d for _ in range(d)]
    f = [[0.0] * d for _ in range(d)]
    h = [[0.0] * d for _ in range(d)]
    for i in range(d):
        h[i][i] = float(n - 2 * i)
        if i >= 1:
            e[i - 1][i] = float(i)
        if i + 1 < d:
            f[i + 1][i] = float(n - i)
    return e, f, h


def demo_module_and_limit() -> None:

    cartan = mat_scale(1.0 / (q - 1 / q), mat_sub(K, Ki))

    print(f"  {'q':>10} | {'|E-e|':>10} {'|F-f|':>10} {'|cartan-h|':>12}")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. The quantum Casimir
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def casimir_scalar(q: float, n: int) -> float:
    """Eigenvalue (q^{n+1} + q^{-(n+1)})/(q - q^-1)^2 of the quantum Casimir."""
    return (q ** (n + 1) + q ** (-(n + 1))) / (q - 1 / q) ** 2


def casimir_regular(q: float, n: int) -> float:
    """Regular form of the shifted eigenvalue: q^{1-n} S_n S_{n+2} / (q+1)^2."""
    sn = sum(q ** i for i in range(n))
    sn2 = sum(q ** i for i in range(n + 2))
    return q ** (1 - n) * sn * sn2 / (q + 1) ** 2


def demo_casimir() -> None:
    print()
    print("=" * 74)
    print("4. THE QUANTUM CASIMIR: SCHUR SCALAR AND CLASSICAL LIMIT")
    print("=" * 74)
    n, q = 3, 1.35
    E, F, K, Ki = uq_module(q, n)
    d = n + 1
    coef = 1.0 / (q - 1 / q) ** 2
    C = mat_add(mat_mul(F, E), mat_scale(coef, mat_add(mat_scale(q, K), mat_scale(1 / q, Ki))))
    lam = casimir_scalar(q, n)
    print(f"  n = {n}, q = {q}:  C - lambda*I  deviation : "
          f"{mat_dist(C, mat_scale(lam, mat_id(d))):.3e}    (lambda = {lam:.6f})")
    print("  => the Casimir acts by ONE scalar on the whole module (quantum Schur)")

    print(f"\n  shifted eigenvalue  Omega_q(n) - (q+q^-1)/(q-q^-1)^2  ->  n(n+2)/4")
    print(f"  {'q':>10} | " + " ".join(f"n={n}".rjust(12) for n in range(1, 5)))
    for q in (1.5, 1.1, 1.01, 1.001):
        shift = (q + 1 / q) / (q - 1 / q) ** 2
        row = " ".join(f"{casimir_scalar(q, n) - shift:12.6f}" for n in range(1, 5))
        print(f"  {q:10.5f} | {row}")
    print(f"  {'limit':>10} | " + " ".join(f"{n * (n + 2) / 4:12.6f}" for n in range(1, 5)))
    q = 1.0001
    err = max(abs(casimir_scalar(q, n) - (q + 1 / q) / (q - 1 / q) ** 2 - casimir_regular(q, n))
              for n in range(1, 5))
    print(f"\n  agreement with the regular form at q = {q} : {err:.3e}"
          "   (regular form is stable, the raw difference is not)")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. Temperley-Lieb, Reidemeister II, Yang-Baxter
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def loop_value(A: complex) -> complex:
    """delta = -A^2 - A^-2."""
    return -A ** 2 - A ** (-2)


def cup(A: complex, i: int, j: int) -> complex:
    """Coefficients of the q-deformed singlet  omega = A|01> - A^-1|10>."""
    if (i, j) == (0, 1):
        return A
    if (i, j) == (1, 0):
        return -1 / A
    return 0.0


def tl_generators_8(A: complex) -> Tuple[Matrix, Matrix]:
    """The 8x8 Temperley-Lieb generators e_1, e_2 on V (x) V (x) V, V = k^2."""
    idx: List[Tuple[int, int, int]] = list(product((0, 1), repeat=3))
    pos: Dict[Tuple[int, int, int], int] = {p: n for n, p in enumerate(idx)}
    e1: Matrix = [[0.0] * 8 for _ in range(8)]
    e2: Matrix = [[0.0] * 8 for _ in range(8)]
    for p in idx:
        for r in idx:
            e1[pos[p]][pos[r]] = -cup(A, p[0], p[1]) * cup(A, r[0], r[1]) * (p[2] == r[2])
            e2[pos[p]][pos[r]] = -cup(A, p[1], p[2]) * cup(A, r[1], r[2]) * (p[0] == r[0])
    return e1, e2


def kauffman(A: complex, e: Matrix) -> Matrix:
    """The braiding g = A*1 + A^-1 e."""
    return mat_add(mat_scale(A, mat_id(len(e))), mat_scale(1 / A, e))


def demo_temperley_lieb() -> None:
    print()
    print("=" * 74)
    print("5. TEMPERLEY-LIEB, REIDEMEISTER II AND THE YANG-BAXTER EQUATION")
    print("=" * 74)
    for A in (2.0, 0.6 + 0.4j, complex(cos(0.7), sin(0.7))):
        e1, e2 = tl_generators_8(A)
        d = loop_value(A)
        s1 = mat_dist(mat_mul(e1, e1), mat_scale(d, e1))
        s2 = mat_dist(mat_mul(e2, e2), mat_scale(d, e2))
        zig = mat_dist(mat_mul(mat_mul(e1, e2), e1), e1)
        zag = mat_dist(mat_mul(mat_mul(e2, e1), e2), e2)
        g1, g2 = kauffman(A, e1), kauffman(A, e2)
        gi1 = mat_add(mat_scale(1 / A, mat_id(8)), mat_scale(A, e1))
        r2 = mat_dist(mat_mul(g1, gi1), mat_id(8))
        ybe = mat_dist(mat_mul(mat_mul(g1, g2), g1), mat_mul(mat_mul(g2, g1), g2))
        print(f"  A = {A!s:>22}   delta = {d:.4f}")

# 6. The bracket and Jones values of the (2,n) torus links
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def b_coeff(A: Fraction, n: int) -> Fraction:
    """b_n, defined by b_0 = 0 and b_{n+1} = A b_n + A^-1 A^n + A^-1 delta b_n."""
    d = -A ** 2 - 1 / A ** 2
    b = Fraction(0)
    for i in range(n):
        b = A * b + A ** i / A + d * b / A
    return b


def bracket(A: Fraction, n: int) -> Fraction:
    """Kauffman bracket of the closure of sigma_1^n (the (2,n) torus link)."""
    d = -A ** 2 - 1 / A ** 2
    return A ** n * d + b_coeff(A, n)


def jones(A: Fraction, n: int) -> Fraction:
    """Writhe-corrected invariant V_n = (-A^-3)^n <n>."""
    return (-1 / A ** 3) ** n * bracket(A, n)


def qtrace_of_braid_power(A: complex, n: int) -> complex:
    """Quantum trace of R^n on V (x) V, with ribbon weight mu = diag(-A^2, -A^-2)."""
    idx: List[Tuple[int, int]] = list(product((0, 1), repeat=2))
    pos = {p: k for k, p in enumerate(idx)}
    e: Matrix = [[0.0] * 4 for _ in range(4)]
    for p in idx:
        for r in idx:
            e[pos[p]][pos[r]] = -cup(A, p[0], p[1]) * cup(A, r[0], r[1])
    R = mat_pow(kauffman(A, e), n)
    mu = [-A ** 2, -A ** (-2)]
    return sum(mu[p[0]] * mu[p[1]] * R[pos[p]][pos[p]] for p in idx)

# 7. Quantum double: racks, conjugation, abelian anyons

def is_self_distributive(elements: Sequence[int], act: Callable[[int, int], int]) -> bool:
    return all(act(x, act(y, z)) == act(act(x, y), act(x, z))
               for x in elements for y in elements for z in elements)


def rack_braid_relation(elements: Sequence[int], act: Callable[[int, int], int]) -> bool:
    def c1(t: Tuple[int, int, int]) -> Tuple[int, int, int]:
        return (act(t[0], t[1]), t[0], t[2])

    def c2(t: Tuple[int, int, int]) -> Tuple[int, int, int]:
        return (t[0], act(t[1], t[2]), t[1])

    return all(c1(c2(c1(t))) == c2(c1(c2(t)))
               for t in product(elements, repeat=3))


def demo_quantum_double() -> None:
    print()
    print("=" * 74)
    print("7. QUANTUM DOUBLE: SELF-DISTRIBUTIVITY, CONJUGATION, MODULARITY")
    print("=" * 74)

    # symmetric group S_3 as permutations of {0,1,2}, conjugation action
    perms: List[Tuple[int, ...]] = sorted(product(range(3), repeat=3))
    perms = [p for p in perms if len(set(p)) == 3]
    index = {p: i for i, p in enumerate(perms)}

    def compose(a: Tuple[int, ...], b: Tuple[int, ...]) -> Tuple[int, ...]:
        return tuple(a[b[i]] for i in range(3))

    def inverse(a: Tuple[int, ...]) -> Tuple[int, ...]:
        out = [0, 0, 0]
        for i, ai in enumerate(a):
            out[ai] = i
        return tuple(out)

    def conj(i: int, j: int) -> int:
        x, y = perms[i], perms[j]
        return index[compose(compose(x, y), inverse(x))]

    elems = list(range(len(perms)))
    print(f"  group S_3 ({len(perms)} elements), action x |> y = x y x^-1")
    print(f"    self-distributive ?      {is_self_distributive(elems, conj)}")
    print(f"    braid relation holds ?   {rack_braid_relation(elems, conj)}")

    # a NON self-distributive operation must fail the braid relation (the 'only if')
    def bad(i: int, j: int) -> int:
        return (i + j) % len(perms)

    print(f"    control: x |> y = x + y  self-distributive ? {is_self_distributive(elems, bad)}"
          f",  braid relation ? {rack_braid_relation(elems, bad)}")

    # abelian anyons: A = Z/N with chi(x,y) = exp(2 pi i x y / N)
    print("\n  abelian anyons  A = Z/N,  chi(x,y) = exp(2 pi i x y / N)")
    for N in (2, 3, 5, 6):
        def chi(x: int, y: int, N: int = N) -> complex:
            return complex(cos(2 * pi * x * y / N), sin(2 * pi * x * y / N))

        # Yang-Baxter for the diagonal braiding
        ybe = max(
            abs(chi(y, x) * chi(z, x) * chi(z, y) - chi(z, y) * chi(z, x) * chi(y, x))
            for x, y, z in product(range(N), repeat=3)
        )
        # hexagons = bilinearity
        hexl = max(abs(chi((x + y) % N, z) - chi(x, z) * chi(y, z))
                   for x, y, z in product(range(N), repeat=3))
        # modularity:  sum_y chi(x,y) chi(-x',y) = N delta_{x,x'}
        worst = 0.0
        for x, xp in product(range(N), repeat=2):
            s = sum(chi(x, y) * chi((-xp) % N, y) for y in range(N))
            target = complex(N if x == xp else 0)
            worst = max(worst, abs(s - target))
        nondeg = all(any(abs(chi(x, y) - 1) > 1e-12 for y in range(N)) for x in range(1, N))
        print(f"    N = {N}:  YBE {ybe:.1e}   hexagon {hexl:.1e}   "
              f"nondegenerate {nondeg}   S S' - N*Id  {worst:.1e}")
    print("  invertible S-matrix  ==>  the braided category is modular")

## A guided tour of quantum groups, braiding, and the invariant that detects the trefoil

There is one idea at the bottom of everything on this page. Take a familiar algebra of
symmetries, introduce a parameter $q$, and bend the multiplication rules by it. At
$q = 1$ you get back exactly what you started with. Away from $q = 1$ you get something
genuinely new: a consistent way of *braiding* objects around each other, which the
classical theory did not have. And braiding, it turns out, is enough to tell knots apart.

We will build the whole story in four steps: the classical algebra, the deformation, the
braiding, and the knot invariant. Interactive panels along the way let you turn the dial
yourself.

---

## 1. The classical world: a ladder of states

The Lie algebra $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ has three generators obeying
$$[h,e] = 2e, \qquad [h,f] = -2f, \qquad [e,f] = h.$$
For each integer $n \ge 0$ there is a representation of dimension $n+1$: a ladder
$v_0, v_1, \dots, v_n$ with
$$e\,v_i = i\,v_{i-1}, \qquad f\,v_i = (n-i)\,v_{i+1}, \qquad h\,v_i = (n-2i)\,v_i .$$
Physically $h$ is a spin projection and $n/2$ is the spin. This is the quantum mechanics
of angular momentum, and it is the object we are about to deform.

<details>
<summary>Why does the ladder close off after $n+1$ rungs?</summary>

Because the coefficient of $f$ vanishes at the bottom: $f\,v_n = (n-n)v_{n+1} = 0$. Try
to push past the last rung and you get zero. The same mechanism will survive the
deformation, with $(n-i)$ replaced by a $q$-weighted version that vanishes at exactly the
same place — which is why the deformed algebra has the *same* list of finite-dimensional
representations as the classical one.
</details>

---

## 2. Bending the rules: the deformation

Replace $h$ by an invertible element $K$ (think "$q^h$") and impose
$$KEK^{-1} = q^2E, \qquad KFK^{-1} = q^{-2}F, \qquad
  EF - FE = \frac{K - K^{-1}}{q - q^{-1}} .$$
That last right-hand side is the crux. At $q = 1$ both its numerator and denominator
vanish. The whole theory hinges on this $0/0$ having a limit — and it does.

The bookkeeping device is the **quantum integer**
$$[m]_q = \frac{q^m - q^{-m}}{q - q^{-1}},$$
which satisfies $[m]_1 = m$ because it can be rewritten without any denominator at all:
$$[m]_q = q^{1-m}\left(1 + q^2 + q^4 + \cdots + q^{2(m-1)}\right).$$

Turn the dial below and watch the deformation dissolve.

{{interactive_demo:0}}

The deformed ladder is the same ladder, re-weighted:
$$E\,v_i = [i]_q\,v_{i-1}, \qquad F\,v_i = [n-i]_q\,v_{i+1},
  \qquad K\,v_i = q^{\,n-2i}v_i .$$
That these operators satisfy all three defining relations is one identity in disguise.

<details>
<summary>Click to reveal the identity that makes it all work</summary>

Everything follows from
$$[a]_q[b]_q - [a-1]_q[b+1]_q = [b-a+1]_q .$$
Setting $a = i$ and $b = n-i$ gives exactly
$[i]_q[n-i+1]_q - [n-i]_q[i+1]_q = [\,n-2i\,]_q$, which is the deformed commutator
$(K - K^{-1})/(q-q^{-1})$ acting on $v_i$. To prove the identity, clear denominators: the
left side becomes $q^{b-a+2} - q^{b-a} + q^{a-b-2} - q^{a-b}$, which is precisely the
expansion of $(q^{b-a+1} - q^{a-b-1})(q - q^{-1})$.
</details>

<details>
<summary>The Casimir: a difference of two infinities that is perfectly finite</summary>

The quantum Casimir is
$C_q = FE + (qK + q^{-1}K^{-1})/(q-q^{-1})^2$; it commutes with $E$, $F$ and $K$, and it
acts on the $(n+1)$-dimensional module by the single scalar
$$\Omega_q(n) = \frac{q^{\,n+1} + q^{-(n+1)}}{(q-q^{-1})^2},$$
independent of which rung you are on — a quantum Schur's lemma. This diverges as
$q \to 1$, but the *normalisation* is what diverges: subtract the value on the trivial
module and you get
$$q^{1-n}\frac{(1+q+\cdots+q^{n-1})(1+q+\cdots+q^{n+1})}{(q+1)^2},$$
which is finite at $q=1$, where it equals $n(n+2)/4$ — the classical total-spin
eigenvalue. The second table in the dial above shows this happening.
</details>

Even the combinatorics deforms in lockstep, through the **Gaussian binomials**
$\binom{n}{j}_q$ defined by the $q$-Pascal rule
$\binom{n+1}{j+1}_q = q^{\,n-j}\binom{n}{j}_q + \binom{n}{j+1}_q$: whenever
$yx = q\,xy$ one has $(x+y)^n = \sum_j \binom{n}{j}_q x^jy^{n-j}$, and at $q=1$ this is
the ordinary binomial theorem. Since $KE = q^2EK$ inside the quantum group, powers of
$E + K$ expand this way too.

## 3. What is genuinely new: exchange that is not a swap

In the classical world, exchanging two tensor factors is a flip, and flipping twice does
nothing. In the deformed world the natural exchange operator $\check R$ obeys the weaker
but far richer **braid relation** (the Yang–Baxter equation)
$$\check R_1\check R_2\check R_1 = \check R_2\check R_1\check R_2 .$$
This is the defining relation of the braid group. Its source is the asymmetry of the
coproduct: $\Delta(E) = E\otimes1 + K\otimes E$ is not symmetric under exchanging the
two factors, and repairing that asymmetry costs you an operator that is no longer an
involution.

Concretely, in the two-dimensional representation the tensor square contains an invariant
**singlet**, but a lopsided one:
$$\omega = A\,|01\rangle - A^{-1}|10\rangle, \qquad q = A^{-2}.$$
Projecting onto it gives an operator $e$ with
$$e^2 = \delta e, \qquad \delta = -A^2 - A^{-2},$$
and on three factors two such projectors satisfy the **Temperley–Lieb relations**
$e_i^2 = \delta e_i$, $e_1e_2e_1 = e_1$, $e_2e_1e_2 = e_2$. The braiding is then
astonishingly simple:
$$g = A\cdot 1 + A^{-1}e .$$

<details>
<summary>Click to reveal the two-line proofs of the braid relation and its inverse</summary>

**Invertibility (Reidemeister II).** With $\bar g = A^{-1} + A\,e$,
$$g\bar g = 1 + (A^2 + A^{-2})e + e^2 = 1 + (A^2 + A^{-2} + \delta)e = 1,$$
using $\delta = -A^2 - A^{-2}$. Note this *forces* the loop value: no other $\delta$
works.

**Braid relation.** Expand the eight terms of $g_1g_2g_1$. Four of them are
$A^3$, $A\,e_2$, $A^{-1}e_1e_2$, $A^{-1}e_2e_1$; the remaining four are multiples of
$e_1$ with total coefficient
$$2A + A^{-1}\delta + A^{-3} = 2A - A - A^{-3} + A^{-3} = A .$$
So $g_1g_2g_1 = A^3 + A e_1 + A e_2 + A^{-1}e_1e_2 + A^{-1}e_2e_1$, which is symmetric in
$e_1 \leftrightarrow e_2$; the same expansion of $g_2g_1g_2$ gives the identical
expression. Hence they are equal.
</details>

Because both identities hold, the assignment $\sigma_i \mapsto g_i$ defines a genuine
representation of the braid group
$B_3 = \langle\sigma_1,\sigma_2 \mid \sigma_1\sigma_2\sigma_1 =
\sigma_2\sigma_1\sigma_2\rangle$. Moreover $g$ commutes with the entire quantum-group
action, so it is a symmetry-respecting operator rather than an ad hoc matrix — the
property that makes the next step well posed. For more background on the algebra of
crossings see the
[Temperley–Lieb algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temperley%E2%80%93Lieb_algebra)
and the [Yang–Baxter equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yang%E2%80%93Baxter_equation).

---

## 4. Closing the braid: a knot invariant

Any knot or link can be drawn as a braid with its ends closed up. To turn a braid matrix
into a number one needs a trace that does not notice the closing-up. The right one is the
**quantum trace**, weighted by $\mu = \mathrm{diag}(-A^2, -A^{-2})$:
$$\mathrm{qtr}(X) = \sum_{i,j}\mu_i\mu_j X_{(ij),(ij)}, \qquad
  \mathrm{qtr}(1) = \delta^2, \quad \mathrm{qtr}(e) = \delta .$$
These two values are exactly what the pictures say: closing the trivial braid gives two
circles, closing $e$ gives one.

Now play. Add crossings, watch the link change, and read off its invariant.

{{interactive_demo:1}}

The algebra behind the panel is short. Since $e^2 = \delta e$, powers of the braiding
stay two-dimensional:
$$g^n = A^n\cdot 1 + b_n\,e, \qquad \delta\,b_n = (-1)^nA^{-3n} - A^n,$$
so the bracket of the closed braid and the writhe-corrected invariant are
$$\langle n\rangle = A^n\delta + b_n, \qquad V_n = (-A^{-3})^n\langle n\rangle .$$

Three values matter:

| $n$ | link | bracket | invariant |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | unknot | $-A^3$ | $V = 1$ |
| 2 | Hopf link | $-A^4 - A^{-4}$ | — |
| 3 | trefoil | $-A^5 - A^{-3} + A^{-7}$ | $V = t + t^3 - t^4$, $\;t = A^{-4}$ |

And the punchline: $t + t^3 - t^4$ is not the constant $1$. At $t = 1/16$ it equals
$4111/65536$. Since the bracket is unchanged by the moves relating different pictures of
the same link — those moves being precisely the two algebraic identities above — the
trefoil is not the unknot. **You cannot untie a trefoil**, and the certificate is a
rational number.

Every deformed quantity is a ratio that degenerates at the classical point, so naive

difference of two numbers of size $(q-1)^{-2}$. The cure is to evaluate the proved

## 5. The wider principle: braiding is everywhere

The braiding above was not a coincidence of one algebra. Here is the same phenomenon in
pure set theory. Call an operation $x \triangleright y$ **self-distributive** if
$$x\triangleright(y\triangleright z) = (x\triangleright y)\triangleright(x\triangleright z),$$
and define $c_1(x,y,z) = (x\triangleright y, x, z)$, $c_2(x,y,z) = (x, y\triangleright z, y)$.
Then $c_1c_2c_1 = c_2c_1c_2$ **if and only if** the operation is self-distributive.
Self-distributivity *is* the braid relation. The canonical example is conjugation
$x \triangleright y = xyx^{-1}$ in any group — the elementary face of the
[Drinfeld quantum double](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_double).

Push one step further, to a finite abelian group $A$ with a bicharacter $\chi$. Braiding
anyons by $x \otimes y \mapsto \chi(y,x)\,y\otimes x$ satisfies Yang–Baxter, the two
bilinearity conditions are the hexagon axioms, and if $\chi$ is nondegenerate then the
matrix $S_{xy} = \chi(x,y)$ satisfies $S\,S' = |A|\cdot\mathrm{Id}$ and is therefore
invertible. Invertibility of $S$ is the definition of a
[modular tensor category](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modular_tensor_category): no
anyon is invisible to the braiding. That is the condition under which such a system can
store and protect quantum information.

## 6. What to take away

- **Nothing is lost in the limit.** Quantum integers become integers, Gaussian binomials
  become binomial coefficients, the deformed ladder becomes the classical ladder, and the
  Casimir eigenvalue becomes $n(n+2)/4$. The classical theory is the $q = 1$ slice.
- **Something is gained away from the limit.** A non-involutive exchange operator
  satisfying the Yang–Baxter equation, hence representations of braid groups.
- **The gain is computable, and it is topology.** Closing two-strand braids gives the
  exact bracket of every $(2,n)$ torus link, correctly normalised to $1$ on the unknot,
  and $t + t^3 - t^4$ on the trefoil — a proof, by arithmetic, that a piece of string
  cannot be untied.

## C1. Reidemeister invariance of the writhe-normalised bracket is *purely* a
`δ = −A² − A^{−2}` fact

**Conjecture.** Let `R` be any algebra containing an element `e` with `e² = δ·e`, and let
`g = A·1 + A^{−1}·e`. Define a Markov-style functional `tr` on the algebra generated by
`g` by `tr(1) = δ`, `tr(e) = 1`. Then the writhe-normalised value
`(−A^{−3})^w · tr(gⁿ)` is invariant under all three Reidemeister moves **if and only if**
`δ = −A² − A^{−2}`; no other normalisation of the loop value, and no extra hypothesis on
`R`, is needed. In particular the "only if" direction is a genuine rigidity statement:
any `δ` making the kink factor consistent is forced.

**The key insight is** that the loop value enters only through the two scalar identities
`A·δ + A^{−1} = −A³` (kink) and `A·A^{−1} + A^{−1}A + A^{−1}δA^{−1} = 0`
(Reidemeister II), which are *simultaneously* solvable for a single `δ` only at
`δ = −A² − A^{−2}`; everything topological is downstream of this two-equation system.

**Why now?** The braiding's invertibility, the braid relation and the quantum trace of
its powers already isolate exactly these scalar identities inside a complete development,
so the conjecture is one uniqueness lemma away from being decidable: solve the two
equations for `δ` and show the solution is unique.

---

## C2. The `(2,n)` torus-link family is *complete* for the Jones polynomial at generic `A`

**Conjecture.** The map `n ↦ V_n(A) = (−A^{−3})^n(A^n δ + b_n)` is injective on `ℕ` for
every transcendental `A`, and moreover already injective at the single rational point
`A = 2` (where `V_1 = 1`, `V_3 = 4111/65536`, `V_5 = 1052431/268435456`, …).
Consequently the Jones polynomial distinguishes *all* `(2,n)` torus links from each
other, provably by a single evaluation.

**The key insight is** that the exact closed form `δ·⟨n⟩ = δ²A^n + (−1)^n A^{−3n} − A^n`
makes `V_n(2)` a strictly monotone-in-modulus sequence of rationals with denominators
`2^{4n}`, so injectivity reduces to an elementary `p`-adic valuation argument rather than
to any topology.

**Why now?** The closed form and the separation `V_1 ≠ V_3` are already proved; upgrading
a single inequality to a full injectivity statement is the natural next target and would
give an infinite family of rigorously distinguished links.

---

## C3. Root-of-unity truncation: the Temperley–Lieb braid representation is unitarisable
exactly on the Jones interval

**Conjecture.** For `A = e^{iθ}` the 8-dimensional Temperley–Lieb representation of the
three-strand braid group carries an invariant Hermitian form which is positive definite
**exactly** when the loop value satisfies `|δ| ≤ 2`, i.e. on the Jones interval of `θ`,
with the form degenerating precisely at the endpoints. This is the algebraic gateway to
the root-of-unity truncation and to the braid representations relevant to topological
quantum computation.

---

## C4. A quantitative classical limit

**Conjecture.** All convergence statements of the degeneration admit uniform first-order
error bounds with explicit constants: `|[m]_q − m| ≤ C_m|q − 1|`, `|C_q(n,j) −

genuine first-order deformation theory, with the derivative at `q = 1` identifying the
canonical Poisson structure on the classical object.

---

## C5. Modularity beyond the pointed case

**Conjecture.** The orthogonality argument establishing that a nondegenerate bicharacter

Grothendieck ring, with `|A|` replaced by `|G|²` divided by the appropriate centraliser

# Gaussian binomial coefficients and the `q`-binomial theorem

This file supplies the *combinatorial* half of the statement "`U_q(g)` is a `q`-deformation of
`U(g)`", complementing the analytic half proved in `Physics.QuantumSL2ClassicalLimit`.

## Contents

* **Gaussian binomials.**  `QuantumBinomial.qBinom q n j` is defined by the `q`-Pascal recursion
  `[n+1 ; j+1] = q^{n-j} [n ; j] + [n ; j+1]`.  We prove the vanishing/normalisation lemmas,
  the closed form `qBinom q n 1 = ∑_{i<n} qⁱ`, and the *second* `q`-Pascal recursion
  `[n+1 ; j+1] = [n ; j] + q^{j+1} [n ; j+1]` (`qBinom_pascal'`), which is a genuine theorem for
  this definition, plus the reflection symmetry `[n ; j] = [n ; n-j]` (`qBinom_symm`).

* **The `q`-binomial theorem.**  `add_pow_of_qCommute`: if `y x = q (x y)` in a `k`-algebra then
  `(x+y)ⁿ = ∑_j [n ; j]_q x^j y^{n-j}`.  This is the deformation of the classical binomial
  theorem, which is recovered at `q = 1` (`qBinom_one_eq_choose`, `add_pow_of_commute_of_qBinom`).

* **Degeneration.**  `qBinom_continuous` and `qBinom_tendsto_choose` show that each Gaussian
  binomial is a polynomial in `q` converging to the ordinary binomial coefficient as `q → 1`,
  so the whole deformed expansion degenerates to the classical one.

* **Bridge to `U_q(sl₂)`.**  `qInt_eq_qBinom` identifies the balanced quantum integer `[m]_q` of
  `Physics.QuantumSL2ClassicalLimit` with `q^{1-m}·[m ; 1]_{q²}`, and `IsUqSl2.add_pow_E_K`
  applies the `q`-binomial theorem to the generators `E, K` of `U_q(sl₂)`, whose relation
  `K E = q² E K` is exactly a `q²`-commutation.
-/

import Mathlib
import Physics.QuantumSL2ClassicalLimit

open Filter Topology

namespace QuantumBinomial

/-! ## 1. Gaussian binomial coefficients -/

section Defs

variable {k : Type*} [CommRing k]

/-- The **Gaussian (`q`-)binomial coefficient** `[n ; j]_q`, defined by the `q`-Pascal
recursion `[n+1 ; j+1] = q^{n-j} [n ; j] + [n ; j+1]`. -/
def qBinom (q : k) : ℕ → ℕ → k
  | _, 0 => 1
  | 0, _ + 1 => 0
  | n + 1, j + 1 => q ^ (n - j) * qBinom q n j + qBinom q n (j + 1)

@[simp] theorem qBinom_zero_right (q : k) (n : ℕ) : qBinom q n 0 = 1 := by
  cases n <;> rfl

@[simp] theorem qBinom_zero_succ (q : k) (j : ℕ) : qBinom q 0 (j + 1) = 0 := rfl

theorem qBinom_succ_succ (q : k) (n j : ℕ) :
    qBinom q (n + 1) (j + 1) = q ^ (n - j) * qBinom q n j + qBinom q n (j + 1) := rfl

/-- Gaussian binomials vanish above the diagonal. -/
theorem qBinom_eq_zero_of_lt (q : k) : ∀ {n j : ℕ}, n < j → qBinom q n j = 0 := by
  intro n
  induction n with
  | zero =>
      intro j hj
      obtain ⟨j, rfl⟩ := Nat.exists_eq_succ_of_ne_zero (by omega : j ≠ 0)
      simp
  | succ n ih =>
      intro j hj
      obtain ⟨j, rfl⟩ := Nat.exists_eq_succ_of_ne_zero (by omega : j ≠ 0)
      rw [qBinom_succ_succ, ih (by omega), ih (by omega)]
      ring

@[simp] theorem qBinom_self (q : k) (n : ℕ) : qBinom q n n = 1 := by
  induction n with
  | zero => simp
  | succ n ih =>
      rw [qBinom_succ_succ, ih, qBinom_eq_zero_of_lt q (by omega : n < n + 1)]
      simp

/-- `[n ; 1]_q = 1 + q + ⋯ + q^{n-1}`, the *unbalanced* quantum integer. -/
theorem qBinom_one (q : k) (n : ℕ) : qBinom q n 1 = ∑ i ∈ Finset.range n, q ^ i := by
  induction n with
  | zero => simp
  | succ n ih =>
      rw [show (1 : ℕ) = 0 + 1 from rfl, qBinom_succ_succ, ih, Finset.sum_range_succ]
      simp [add_comm]

/-- **The second `q`-Pascal recursion.**  With the definition above (which builds in
`[n+1 ; j+1] = q^{n-j}[n ; j] + [n ; j+1]`), the dual recursion is a theorem. -/
theorem qBinom_pascal' (q : k) : ∀ (n j : ℕ),
    qBinom q (n + 1) (j + 1) = qBinom q n j + q ^ (j + 1) * qBinom q n (j + 1) := by
  intro n
  induction n with

      | 0 => simp

  | succ n ih =>

      | 0 =>

            Finset.sum_range_succ _ _

          simp only [qBinom_one, qBinom_zero_right, Nat.sub_zero, mul_one, pow_one, zero_add]
          linear_combination h1 - h2
      | (j + 1) =>

            have e1 : n + 1 - (j + 1) = n - (j + 1) + 1 := by omega

  intro n

      match j with
      | 0 => simp
      | (j + 1) =>
          have hj' : j ≤ n := by omega
          have e0 : n + 1 - (j + 1) = n - j := by omega

          rcases Nat.eq_or_lt_of_le hj' with heq | hlt

            simp

            have e2 : n - (n - j - 1) = j + 1 := by omega

            have e6 : n - j - 1 + 1 = n - j := by omega

theorem qpow_comm {q : k} {x y : R} (h : y * x = q • (x * y)) :

theorem qBinom_one_eq_choose (n j : ℕ) : qBinom (1 : k) n j = (n.choose j : k) := by
  induction n generalizing j with

  | succ n ih =>

      | succ j => rw [qBinom_succ_succ, ih, ih, Nat.choose_succ_succ]; push_cast; ring

theorem add_pow_of_commute_of_qBinom {x y : R} (h : y * x = x * y) (n : ℕ) :
    (x + y) ^ n = ∑ j ∈ Finset.range (n + 1), (n.choose j : k) • (x ^ j * y ^ (n - j)) := by
